summary: In deep-space exploration missions, prolonged exposure to microgravity and radiation can affect crew health. Due to significant communication delays and lack of medical personnel, autonomous clinical monitoring is crucial. This work presents BayMex, a hybrid monitoring and decision-support system developed for Earth-Independent Medical Operations (EIMO). It features a physical prototype using Arduino UNO to capture vital signs and environmental data, performing triage through a color-coded system. Additionally, it includes a software architecture with an SQLite database, a Python-based REST API, and a cross-platform mobile app. Validation tests demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing cognitive load and facilitating crew monitoring and emergency response during missions.
details: BayMex is a biomedical monitoring and decision-support ecosystem designed to support the medical autonomy of crews on long-duration space missions. A sensor device captures each astronaut's vital signs and environmental data (heart rate, sleep, body temperature, hydration, stress, blood oxygen saturation, and radiation dose) and classifies them immediately with a green, yellow, or red triage code. The data is stored in a local database and served through a Python API to a cross-platform mobile app, where each astronaut can check their own information at any time: the current value of each indicator, its normal range, its history, and recommendations. When an indicator becomes critical, the app presents step-by-step physical and emotional emergency protocols, so the crew can act without waiting for Mission Control, while administrators get a crew-wide dashboard that prioritizes who needs attention and why. In this stage, an Arduino prototype emulates the sensor capture and all data is fictitious; connecting real sensors to the server is the next phase. The main benefits are that it turns raw numbers into clear states and actions, reducing cognitive overload and alarm fatigue; it lets crews monitor themselves when communication with Earth is delayed by up to 24 minutes or interrupted; it gives the medical team a single, traceable view of the whole crew; and it protects privacy through role-based access and administrator approval of every account. Its intended impact is to support Earth-Independent Medical Operations (EIMO) in missions such as Artemis and future trips to Mars, helping crews detect problems early and respond before they become emergencies, and to serve as a training simulator for analog missions. We built the app with Flutter and Dart, the backend with Python and FastAPI, and the database with SQLite inspected in DB Browser; the hardware prototype uses an Arduino UNO programmed in C++ with a 16x2 LCD, a potentiometer, a push button, and an RGB LED, housed in an enclosure designed in SolidWorks and 3D printed; and we tested the system with pytest, a Flutter unit test, and an Android APK installed on a phone and connected to the backend through an HTTPS tunnel. The project is creative because it pairs a physical device that gives instant visual triage on its own with a software layer that explains the situation and says what to do, includes interactive protocols for emotional crises and not only physical ones, and keeps clinical thresholds in the database so they can be adjusted without rebuilding the app. Along the way we considered the communication delay and the absence of a physician onboard, the cognitive load of crews working under sleep deprivation, the effects of isolation and confinement on mental health, privacy and identity verification, and the importance of being honest about limits: the app is decision support and not a diagnosis, its guidance is reference material pending validation by the medical team, and we recommend at least two administrators onboard to keep supervision going if the mission leader is incapacitated.
